system:
You audit the knowledge atoms of one Knowledge Card. A card is the answer key for a benchmark of expert conceptual knowledge, so every atom must be correct, self-contained, and assessable on its own.

Judge every atom on every check listed below. Rules:
- For checks about evidence, use only the evidence sentences supplied with the atom. Do not repair an atom with your own knowledge.
- For GROUNDED, use "hold" when unreadable PDF symbols prevent verification; explain what is needed. Use fail only when the available evidence is sufficient to determine that the claim is unsupported. This hold rule takes precedence over the strictness rule. Judge other checks independently using their listed values; do not invent missing facts.
- Be strict within each check's allowed values. Do not turn an inability to verify GROUNDED into revise or fail; use hold as defined above.
- "why" is required for every value other than the first listed value; keep it under 30 words. Omit "why" when passing.

Checks (allowed values in brackets; the first value means no problem):
- GROUNDED [pass / revise / fail / hold]: The cited evidence sentences state the atom, including its specificity, causal force, assumptions, and certainty. pass = fully stated. revise = partly stated (the atom adds, drops, or strengthens something; say what). fail = not stated when the available evidence permits a judgment. hold = unreadable symbols prevent verification. For pass or revise, put the supporting evidence ids in cite.
- SINGLE_CLAIM [pass / revise]: The atom is one independently assessable claim. revise = it joins two or more claims that could be true or false separately. Evidence spanning more than three sentences is not by itself a reason to split or revise an atom.
- SCOPE_LABEL [pass / revise]: The S label fits (S1 what it is / S2 how it works / S3 where it ends). revise = wrong label; put the right one in why, e.g. 'S2: ...'.
- L1_ONLY [pass / fail]: The atom is recall-level knowledge. fail = knowing it requires applying the concept to a new problem, or combining facts from distant passages.
- SOURCE_INDEPENDENT [pass / revise / fail]: A domain expert who never read this book could judge the claim true or false. revise = phrased as the authors' statement but the claim itself is general (drop the attribution). fail = an isolated study finding, conjecture, or author-specific opinion, classification, or recommendation, even if attribution was removed. Explicitly scoped established facts about a formalism or architecture and conditional theoretical results remain eligible.
- NO_OVERLAP [pass / fail]: No other atom in this card states or contains the same claim. If two atoms overlap, fail only the less informative one and put the other atom's id in cite; the other one passes.
- CENTRALITY [pass / fail]: The atom matters for understanding the concept. fail = peripheral detail.
Whole-card checks (report under "batch"):
- CONCEPT_SCOPE [pass / fail]: The concept is a general concept of the field. fail = a topic whose assessable content is restricted to excluded study-specific findings or author-specific positions. A named formalism, system, or architecture is not disqualified solely for being specific if its scoped conceptual facts are source-independent.

Output ONLY one JSON object:
{"units": {"<atom_id>": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": "", "cite": []}, ...}, ...}, "batch": {"<CHECK>": {"v": "<value>", "why": ""}}}

CONCEPT: Preferential attachment sampling
ASSESSMENT SCOPE: Reduction of dynamic weighted sampling in the BA model to uniform edge-list sampling. Also I/O-efficient variants and the hash-based copy scheme of CA-BA.

ATOMS:
- CS-ALG-C09-S1-01 | S1
  ATOM: Preferential attachment is a positive feedback loop in dynamic systems in which selecting an item at one point in time increases the probability of selecting it again in the future.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s04] At its core, their BA model relies on preferential attachment, a positive feedback loop in dynamic systems where selecting an item at one point in time increases the probability of selecting it again in the future.
- CS-ALG-C09-S1-02 | S1
  ATOM: In the Barabási–Albert (BA) model, one starts from a seed graph $G_0$ with $n_0$ vertices and $m_0$ edges and adds $n-n_0$ nodes one at a time. Each new node chooses $d$ neighbors at random, with the probability of selecting a node $v$ proportional to the degree of $v$ at that time.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s07] Starting with an arbitrary seed graph G0 with n0 vertices and m0 edges, we iteratively add n −n0 nodes—one node at a time.
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s08] For each new node, we choose d neighbors at random where the probability to select node v is proportional to the degree of v at that time.
- CS-ALG-C09-S1-03 | S1
  ATOM: The main algorithmic challenge of generating BA graphs is the dynamic weighted sampling of neighbors.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s09] The main algorithmic challenge of BA lies in this dynamic weighted sampling.
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-01.r1a | S2
  ATOM: In preferential attachment sampling for the BA model, each node of degree $k$ appears exactly $k$ times in the edge list produced so far, so the dynamic weighted sampling problem reduces to uniformly selecting entries from the edge list.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s11] Batagelj and Brandes [6] observe that each node with degree k appears exactly k-times in the edge list produced so far.
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s12] Therefore, the underlying dynamic weighted sampling problem can be reduced to uniformly selecting entries from the edge list, leading to the linear-time generator BB-BA.
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-01.r1b | S2
  ATOM: The reduction of dynamic weighted sampling to uniform selection from the edge list leads to BB-BA, a linear-time generator for the BA model.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s12] Therefore, the underlying dynamic weighted sampling problem can be reduced to uniformly selecting entries from the edge list, leading to the linear-time generator BB-BA.
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-02.r1a | S2
  ATOM: In CA-BA, neighbor sampling uses a shared random hash function $h(\cdot)$ with $h(i)<i$, and the neighbor written at position $i$ of the conceptual edge list is conceptually copied from position $j=h(i)$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s13] Sampling random neighbors involves a shared random hash function h(·) with the property that h(i) < i.
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s14] Then, in order to choose the node index of the random neighbor to be written to the edge list’s i-th position, we conceptually copy the value from position j = h(i).
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-02.r1b | S2
  ATOM: In CA-BA, if $j=h(i)$ satisfies $j\ge 2m_0$ and $j$ is odd, the sampling is retraced by recursing on $j'=h(j)=h(h(i))$.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s14] Then, in order to choose the node index of the random neighbor to be written to the edge list’s i-th position, we conceptually copy the value from position j = h(i).
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s20] If j ≥2m0 and j is odd, we retrace the sampling carried out.
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s21] To do so, we recurse on j′ = h(j) = h(h(i)).
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-03.r1a | S2
  ATOM: Instead of reading from random positions in the edge list, TFP-BA first precomputes all necessary read operations and sorts them by the memory address they read from.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s17] Rather than reading from random positions in the edge list, TFP-BA ﬁrst pre- computes all necessary read operations and sorts them by the memory address they read from.
- CS-ALG-C09-S2-03.r1b | S2
  ATOM: While TFP-BA produces the edge list monotonously from beginning to end, it scans the sorted read requests and forwards the still-cached values to the target positions using an I/O-efficient priority queue.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s18] As the algorithm produces the edge list monotonously moving from beginning to end, it scans through the sorted read request and forwards the still cached values to the target positions using an I/O-efﬁcient priority queue.
- CS-ALG-C09-S3-01 | S3
  ATOM: BB-BA requires unstructured I/Os, so it cannot efficiently produce graphs that do not fit into main memory.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0038-s13] As BB-BA requires unstructured I/Os, it cannot efﬁciently produce graphs that do not ﬁt into main memory.
- CS-ALG-C09-S3-02.r1 | S3
  ATOM: Assuming $h(\cdot)$ can be evaluated in constant time, CA-BA requires expected linear work.
  EVIDENCE:
    [CS-ALG-p0039-s25] Assuming h(·) can be evaluated in constant time, CA-BA therefore requires expected linear work.
